Vacuum Batch Distillation Ver 1 · Student edition

00:00:00 Boiling Score 100 Student edition

How to use the simulator

Operator training simulator of a pilot-scale vacuum batch distillation column (C-101) that separates methyl palmitate (C16:0) from palm-oil biodiesel by a campaign of cuts: off-cut, product cut, residue. Design case: the Aspen optimum of the project (170 mbar pot, 3 kW, R 15 then R 10).

1 Quick start · 2 Top bar · 3 Tabs · 4 DCS console · 5 Faceplates · 6 Trends and alarms · 7 SIS-100 and campaign · 8 Field and lab · 9 Exercises · 10 Debrief and data export · 11 Symbols and colours

1 · Quick start

  1. Click anywhere once so the browser allows alarm sound. Check the top bar shows 🔔 Sound on.
  2. The session opens at the start of a campaign: 110 L charged, column at total reflux, 160 mbar at the top, 3 kW in the pot. Read the Process tab, then open P&ID and DCS console.
  3. A campaign takes about 15 simulated hours: use Speed 20×–100× and Freeze while you think.
  4. Go to Exercises, pick a list (Training, Think EQUIPPED, Procedures) and load an exercise. A blue banner gives the situation; click Acknowledge on the banner to hide it.
  5. Operate from the DCS console (click a bubble for its faceplate) and from the SIS-100 and campaign tab (heating, reflux ratio, distillate route). Take lab samples on Field and lab.
  6. When finished, open Debrief and grading, then Data export for CSV files.

2 · Top bar

ControlWhat it does
ClockSimulated time since the session or exercise started (hh:mm:ss).
Freeze / RunPauses and resumes the simulation.
Speed1× to 100× real time. Grading uses simulated time.
Status lampGreen: heating armed (boiling, total reflux / off-cut / product cut). Amber: heating not armed. Red: SIS-100 tripped. Click it to open the SIS-100 tab.
🔔 Sound · Silence · AcknowledgeAudible alarm on/off; silence the sound only; acknowledge every alarm. One beep = new alarm; two alternating tones = trip, pump running dry or air in the hot column.
ScoreContinuous score for this session (starts at 100).

4 · DCS console

  • Overview: every instrument and a summary at top left (campaign phase and clock, duty and boil-up, receivers, SIS state and configuration).
  • Temperature profile: the 20 stage temperatures and the pot against the start-of-campaign profile (dashed). The light/C16 and C16/C18 fronts show as steps that move up the column.
  • Vacuum and condenser: pressures, PV-102 bleed, VP-101, condenser load vs capacity, condensed fraction, water, and ester lost to the vacuum trap.
  • Campaign and receivers: phase, clock, R, diverter, flows, receiver masses, last lab result and productivity.

Instrument bubbles follow ISA style: letters on top (PIC = pressure indicating controller), loop number below, live value beside or under the bubble. Controllers show MAN, AUTO or CAS at upper right. Red = in alarm; flashing = not acknowledged. A square frame marks a trip (TSHH, PSHH, FSLL, LSLL). Click a bubble, a pump, HV-105 or HV-110 for its faceplate; RY-104 and HS-107 open the reflux-ratio and diverter faceplates.

  • Trend groups: Campaign; Column hydraulics; Vacuum and condenser; Hot oil and pot; Distillate quality (model truth, for the debrief); Selected tag.
  • Window: 10 min to 12 h. Each pen has its own range (legend).
  • Alarm summary: newest unacknowledged first; click a row to acknowledge it and open that instrument.

Button / panelWhat it does

8 · Field and lab

  • Pumps: VP-101 vacuum, P-108 tempered water, P-101 hot oil, P-104 reflux. A tripped motor will not restart until the fault is cleared; P-104 will not start with D-104 almost empty.
  • HV-110 N₂ vacuum break (only below 150 °C). HV-104 hot-oil cooler E-104 for the cool-down.
  • Sight glasses and condenser / vacuum pump checks: what a field operator sees, hears and smells.
  • Lab GC samples: D-105 distillate, TK-201, TK-202, pot. The result (C≤C14, C16:0, C18+) arrives 10 simulated minutes later as a banner, in the table and in the log.

9 · Exercises

  • Load an exercise from Training, Think EQUIPPED or Procedures. The plant is reset to the exercise's starting state (total reflux, mid off-cut, end of off-cut, mid product cut, late product cut, end of campaign, or cold); faults appear on their own schedule.
  • Procedure tracker: steps tick with their time when the simulator sees them done; "!" marks a step done out of order. The campaign procedure is graded on TK-202 purity, product mass, productivity and safety.
  • What-if, trend matching, scrambles and the DCS reading sheet are graded into the Debrief tab.

10 · Debrief and data export

  • Debrief: score and deductions, campaign results (product, purity, recovery, productivity), exercise grades, fault recovery times, event log.
  • Data export: tick data sets, choose range and interval, download. The claude.ai page asks you to confirm each file; on GitHub Pages it downloads directly.

Nothing is stored after you close or reload the page. Download your CSV files before leaving.

1 · What a PFD adds to the BFD

  • Equipment, not blocks: the "D-104 reflux drum" block becomes D-104, the pump P-104, a tee, FV-104 on the reflux and FV-105 on the distillate, and the diverter XV-107.
  • All process streams, numbered left to right, including the ones inside a block (pot ↔ reboiler loop, trap → pump → vent, the hot-oil loop).
  • Information flags (Turton shapes: parallelogram mass flow, rectangle temperature, trapezoid pressure, double chevron volume flow) with the design data.
  • The control valves that define the process: TV-101 (duty), FV-104/FV-105 (reflux split), PV-102 (pressure), and the diverter XV-107 (cut routing).
  • Utilities named on each exchanger: electric power on HE-101, cooling water on E-104, tempered water on E-103, hot oil on D-102.

Operating windows · vacuum batch column C-101

1 Operability of a batch column · 2 Variables and variability · 3 Bounds · 4 Type I: hold map · 5 Type II/III: campaign map · 6 Worst cases and live check · 7 Capacity and turndown · 8 Monte Carlo · 9 Holes and limitations

1 · Operability of a batch column

Operability is the ability of the unit to reach its targets for every disturbance it will meet, without breaking a limit. The operating window is the set of handle settings (and disturbance values) for which that is true. Four things set it: the variability the unit must absorb, the bounds it must respect, the capacity of its equipment and the flexibility (spare range) of its handles.

C-101 is a batch column. It never lines out: the pot gets heavier, the pot temperature climbs and the top composition moves through two cuts. A steady-state window does not exist, so every idea is restated over the campaign:

2 · Variables and variability

Design-basis memorandum: the five sources of variability C-101 must absorb.

3 · Bounds (limits on the trajectory)

A campaign is inside the window when every bound below holds over the whole trajectory: the worst value from the start of the off-cut to the end of the product cut. A Type I hold is judged on the worst value of its last . The margin is normalised (slack ÷ scale): 1 means a comfortable distance, 0 means on the limit, negative means violated. Capacity and hard bounds are listed before "CV not reached", so the first violated bound is the root cause.

4 · Type I: hold map at total reflux (duty × top pressure)

Each cell is one model run from the design state: JIC-101 and PIC-102 set points held, XV-107 CLOSED (total reflux), trips switched off so the limits can be seen (in the plant SIS-100 would act first). This is the hydraulic window of the column itself, before any distillate is drawn.

5 · Type II/III: campaign map (duty × product-cut reflux ratio)

Each cell is one full campaign (feed A, 160 mbar, off-cut R1 15, switch at 4 % light esters in D-104, stop when TK-202 falls below 99.0 %). Here the bounds apply to the trajectory and two more bounds count: the product must reach the specification and the productivity CAP must meet the throughput target.

Other campaigns on the model (pressure, feed B, single disturbances and a combined worst case):

6 · Worst-case presets and a live single-campaign check

Choose a preset or move the sliders, then run one full campaign on the model (about 6 s; trips off so every limit is seen). The result lists every bound with its worst value along the trajectory.

7 · Capacity and turndown

The column is a "series plant": the duty is allowed only where every bound allows it. Each bar is the duty range one bound allows along a row of the Type I map; the overlap is the window, and its ends give the capacity (top) and the turndown (bottom).

8 · Monte Carlo on the campaign map

Set points are not held exactly from campaign to campaign (meter error, operator choice). Sample the duty and R2 from normal distributions and interpolate the campaign margin bilinearly on the Type II/III grid: the share of samples with margin ≥ 0 is the chance that a campaign stays inside.

9 · Holes check and limitations

Teaching deck: Flexibility (32 slides)   Open on claude.ai Open the file (the file link works when the deck sits in the same folder, e.g. GitHub Pages)

Flexibility · handles and spare capacity of C-101

1 What flexibility is · 2 Register of handles · 3 How many: n ≥ m · 4 Where: gains and interaction · 5 Installed characteristics · 6 Production-rate handle · 7 How much is used · 8 Recommendations

1 · What flexibility is

Flexibility is the spare range built into the handles so the operating window of the Operating windows tab can be reached and held for every disturbance: valves that are not wide open, utilities that are not at their limit, pumps with spare flow, controllers with somewhere to go. Without it, the first disturbance takes a handle to its stop and a bound is lost. Three questions organise the tab: how many handles (n ≥ m), where they act (gains and interaction) and how much range each one has (capacity minus what the campaign uses).

For a batch column the answers change along the campaign: the pot gets heavier and hotter, so the same duty needs a wider TV-101 opening late in the cut, and the condenser load moves from light esters (TI-104 ≈ 192 °C) to C16:0 (≈ 250 °C). Every number below is from the model at the start (total reflux) and in the product cut, labelled.

2 · Register of handles and spare capacity

3 · How many handles: n ≥ m

4 · Where the handles act: +5 % open-loop gains

Each handle is moved +5 % (set points: 5 % of their value; hand valves: 5 % points) and held 30 min. The gain is the difference to a run without the step from the same state, because the batch keeps moving. Loops other than the one stepped stay in AUTO, as the operator sees them.

Interaction: 2 × 2 relative gain array (product cut) for the duty Q (JIC-101 SP) and the reflux ratio R (RY-104).

5 · Installed characteristics (the model's own relations)

Duty vs TV-101 opening. TV-101 is equal-percentage with rangeability R = 30 (the model: hot-oil flow·cp = 0.75·30(v/100 − 1) kW/K) feeding reboiler D-102 (UA 0.5 kW/K): Q = ε·ṁcp·(Toil − Tpot), ε = 1 − e−UA/ṁcp.

Condenser E-103 capacity vs HV-105 opening and tempered-water temperature. Capacity = UAc·(opening/50)0.6·(Tdew − Twater)·2.5 (the factor 2.5 is assumed in the model).

HAZID · hazard identification of the vacuum batch still C-101

Plant-level, checklist-driven look at what can hurt people, the plant or the environment on this pilot unit. Risk on the example 5×5 matrix (R = S × L, with the existing safeguards); trip settings and alarm limits are read from the simulator's model. Failure likelihoods are judgement (assumed), not data.

1 What HAZID is · 2 Method · 3 PFD and study areas · 4 Guideword checklist · 5 Hazard register · 6 Major accident hazards · 7 From HAZID to HAZOP and other studies

1 · What HAZID is and where it sits

A HAZID is an early brainstorm on the PFD and the plot plan: what can go wrong at plant level, before the detailed design exists. A HAZOP comes later and asks how each line and vessel can deviate from its design intent, line by line on the P&ID. On a batch unit both are asked per phase of the batch: charging, heat-up, total reflux, off-cut, product cut, shutdown, vacuum break and discharge.

HAZIDHAZOP
WhenConcept / FEED, and again before start-up of a pilotDetailed design (P&ID frozen), and after changes
DrawingPFD (VBD-PFD-100) and the building layoutP&ID (the P&ID tab)
BreakdownAreas (7 here)Nodes (N1–N8)
PromptGuideword checklist by hazard categoryGuide word × parameter (No flow, More temperature …)
ScopeProcess, utilities, building, people, environment, external eventsProcess deviations and operability
OutputHazard register, major accident hazards (MAH), list of further studiesDeviation worksheet, recommendations, input to LOPA and SIL
ReferenceISO 17776IEC 61882

2 · Method

  1. Scope: the pilot vacuum batch still C-101 from the charge in D-101 to the receivers TK-201/TK-202, with the hot-oil skid, the vacuum system, tempered water, N₂, power and the building.
  2. Areas: seven study areas on the PFD (part 3).
  3. Guideword checklist per area: twelve categories (part 4).
  4. Existing controls, split as on a bow-tie: prevention (stops the top event: design, alarms, permissives, procedures) and mitigation (limits the consequence: trips, drip trays, PPE, emergency response).
  5. Rank each hazard on the 5×5 matrix with the existing controls, and flag major accident hazards (here: S ≥ 4, fire or serious injury).
  6. Actions and further studies (HAZOP node, LOPA, SIL, layout, job safety analysis).

HAZOP · Vacuum Batch Distillation Ver 1

HAZOP report (PDF) · document VBD-SA-HZP-001 rev A: close-out summary, method, findings, worksheets of all nodes, drawings and one action sheet per recommendation, built from the same data as this tab. Open the HAZOP report

A teaching HAZOP of the pilot vacuum batch column C-101, done the way a plant team would do it (IEC 61882) and restated for a batch: the guide words are asked of every node and, in node N8, of every batch phase. The risk matrix is an example matrix shared with the HAZID, Safety layers and LOPA tabs. Numbers in the worksheets (alarm limits, trip settings, design values) are read from the model of this page.

1 Standard and method · 2 Team and documents · 3 Nodes · 4 Guide words and parameters · 5 Risk matrix · 6 Worksheets · 7 Coverage · 8 Recommendations · 9 Dynamic check · 10 Follow-up

1 · Standard and method

The study runs in four phases. Definition: scope and boundary — from the charge in D-101 to the receivers TK-201 / TK-202, the hot-oil loop from HE-101 to D-102, the tempered-water loop at E-103 and the vacuum system to the VP-101 exhaust; the feed preparation (biodiesel plant), the hot-oil and tempered-water heaters' own controls, and the building are outside. Preparation: the tabs of this page are the study documents (Part 2); nodes are fixed (Part 3). Examination: the loop below, node by node. Documentation and follow-up: worksheets (Part 6), the recommendation register (Part 8), the report PDF and close-out (Part 10).

The study uses full recording (every meaningful deviation is written down, also when the risk is low) and judges consequences with no credit for safeguards; the likelihood L is then judged with the existing safeguards in place.

2 · Team and documents

3 · Nodes

One node per design intent; a boundary is drawn where the intent changes (pump, exchanger, control valve, the column, the vacuum pump). Node N8 holds the procedures: the guide words are asked of each batch phase.

4 · Guide words and parameters

The eleven IEC 61882 guide words, each with an example row from this study. A deviation is recorded only when it is physically meaningful for the node.

9 · Dynamic check on the simulator

A HAZOP team judges consequences on paper. Here twelve deviations were also run on copies of the model (never the live simulator) for 30 min each, with every alarm and trip active and no operator action. Alarms are evaluated every second exactly as the DCS console does (same limits, suppression and dead band); times are mm:ss after the deviation starts. Safety layers · Vacuum batch still C-101

The protection layers of the unit, from the process design outwards: BPCS → alarms → SIS → relief → containment → emergency response. The drawing is P&ID VBD-V1-PID-001 redrawn layer by layer. 1 · The six layers

Each ring must hold when the one inside it fails. Click a ring to open that layer on the P&ID (part 2, focus view).

Layers 1–3 all need power and computing: one power or DCS failure is a common cause for all of them. That is why the SIS is de-energise to trip and its valves fail safe (XV-101 fail closed), and why layers 4–6, which need neither, are kept in reserve.

2 · P&ID layer by layer

Step through the layers. Step 0 shows the equipment, piping and hand valves; each step adds one layer in its colour. At step 2 the alarm letters replace the loop letters on the same bubbles (TIC → TICAH) and the limit is written beside the bubble. Click any item for its card.

Dashed squares = SIS trips; a short dashed link joins a trip to the transmitter it shares. Rings mark existing valves that the SIS also drives (TV-101, XV-107) and the recommended HV-110 interlock.

Register by layer

3 · What each layer does

Follows the step selected in part 2.

Layer 3 · cause-and-effect matrix of SIS-100

Every cause runs the same trip routine: any SIF or HS-100 trips the whole heating system. What is not stopped matters too: VP-101, P-108, P-101 and P-104 keep running so the condenser and the hot-oil loop cool the still down at total reflux.

Live: ACTIVE = the condition is true now (with its timer against the delay); FIRST-OUT = the cause that tripped SIS-100 (after a trip the conditions clear because heating stops, so the first-out is what stays). PSHH-102, FSLL-108 and LSLL-101 are armed only in RUN; TSHH-101 and TSHH-107 are always armed and block the reset while high. LSLL-104 (P-104 protection) is an equipment interlock, not a SIF.

    A trip may share a sensor with its own alarm, but a trip that shares the control or indication transmitter is not independent: one failure of that transmitter blinds the loop, the alarm and the trip together.

    LOPA · Reliability for safety, layer of protection analysis and bow-tie

    Three parts on the vacuum batch column C-101. Part A turns failure rates into the probability that a safety function fails on demand. Part B uses those numbers to ask whether the protection layers of each hazardous scenario are enough. Part C draws the same layers as a bow-tie. Every failure rate, initiating-event frequency and conditional modifier on this tab is an assumed teaching value unless a source is named; the trip settings, delays and shared sensors are those of SIS-100 in the simulator.

    A Reliability for safety (definitions · population lab · PFD and proof test · RBD · SIF calculator · parallel method · failure data) · B LOPA (chain · five steps · lecture example · criteria · IPL rules · worksheet · register) · C Bow-tie

    Part A · Reliability for safety

    A1 · Definitions, with examples from this unit

    A2 · Population lab: where a failure rate comes from

    One hundred identical devices (think of the 100 thermocouples of a large plant, or 100 bulbs) start together at t = 0. Their lives follow a Weibull distribution: reliability R(t) = exp(−(t/α)β). The lives are the 100 quantiles ti = α(−ln(1 − (i − 0.5)/100))1/β, shuffled with a fixed seed so the picture stays the same. Move t and watch survivors Ns, failed Nf and those failing in the next interval ΔNf; the failure rate is λ = ΔNf/(NsΔt).

    A3 · Probability of failure on demand and proof testing

    A safety device fails dangerously and silently: nobody knows until the next proof test (interval T) or a real demand. With a constant dangerous-undetected rate λ, the unavailability grows as 1 − e−λt and drops back to zero at each test. The average over the interval is PFDavg = 1 − (1 − e−λT)/(λT) ≈ λT/2 when λT ≪ 1.

    A4 · Reliability block diagrams

    A5 · SIF calculator: SIS-100 trips as sensor → logic → final element

    Each SIF is a series of subsystems; its PFDavg is the sum of theirs. Rates are SIS-grade dangerous-undetected rates (assumed, SIL-rated devices with diagnostics), not the generic all-mode rates of A7. Change the voting, a rate or the test interval and see which subsystem dominates.

    A6 · The course parallel method (MTTF of redundant branches)

    A7 · Failure data

    Part B · Layer of protection analysis

    B1 · The LOPA chain

    B2 · Five steps

    1. Pick a scenario from the HAZOP: one cause–consequence pair (nodes N1–N8), and give the consequence a severity S from the criteria (B4). S sets the target frequency.
    2. Initiating event frequency (IEF, /yr) for each cause, from failure data or human-error rates; add enabling conditions (the plant state that must exist for the cause to matter).
    3. Independent protection layers: list every safeguard and keep only those that meet the IPL rules (B5) for that cause. Give each a PFD.
    4. Mitigated frequency f = Σ IEF × enabling × ΠPFD × conditional modifiers (ignition, occupancy). Compare with the target: RRF = f / target.
    5. Decide: RRF ≤ 1 is tolerable; otherwise add a layer with PFD ≤ 1/RRF (an alarm or BPCS layer gives 0.1; a SIF needs the SIL that matches 1/RRF) and record the recommendation.

    B3 · The lecture example

    B4 · Course risk criteria and matrix

    B5 · IPL rules and PFD credits

    B6 · LOPA worksheet for C-101

    Choose a scenario. Recommended layers start unticked (base case = the plant as built in the simulator). A layer that is not independent of a cause is struck through on that cause's row; a recommended layer that supersedes another switches the old one off. Conditional modifiers are editable.

    B7 · LOPA register

    Part C · Bow-tie

    The bow-tie puts the threats (causes) on the left, the top event (the moment control is lost) in the middle and the consequences on the right. Prevention barriers sit between threats and the top event; mitigation barriers and conditional modifiers between the top event and the consequences. Barrier colours follow the safety layers (grey = procedure or conditional modifier); a dashed barrier is recommended and not fitted. Click a barrier to fail it. Escalation factors defeat named barriers.

    SRS of SIF · Safety requirements specification of SIS-100

    1 Where the SRS sits · 2 SIF list · 3 Requirements per SIF · 4 Common requirements · 5 Findings

    1 · Where the SRS sits in the safety life cycle

    IEC 61511-1 clause 10 asks for a written specification of every safety instrumented function before it is designed: what it protects against, what it measures, its set point, the safe state, how fast it must act, how reliable it must be (SIL) and how it is tested, bypassed and reset. The HAZOP finds the scenarios, LOPA decides which need a SIF and how good it must be, and the SRS turns that into requirements the designer, the tester and the operator can check.

    2 · SIF list

    PFDavg is computed live from the LOPA tab's SIF data (SIS-grade λDU, assumed). The process safety time (PST) is measured on this model: a copy loaded with a saved state, every trip disabled, the demand applied, logged every 0.25 s until the hazard criterion; PST = time of the hazard − time the trip point is crossed. Response = sensor 0.5 s + logic 0.25 s + on-delay + valve 2 s (assumed). The Live column reads the running simulator.

    1 What a C&E diagram is · 2 The diagram · 3 How to read a row · 4 Notes · 5 Checks against the simulator

    1 · What a cause and effect diagram is

    A cause and effect (C&E) matrix is the shortest complete statement of what a safety system does. Each row is a cause: an instrument crossing a setting (with its direction and on-delay), a push-button or a sequence condition. Each column is an effect: a valve closing, a heater switching off, an alarm, a first-out lamp. A mark where they cross means "this cause does this effect". Designers write the logic from it, testers tick it off during the site acceptance test, and operators read it to see why the unit stopped. It does not say why a trip exists (that is the HAZOP and LOPA) or how fast and how reliable it must be (that is the SRS).

    Efficiency · vacuum batch column C-101

    How well does one campaign turn electricity, column-hours and charged C16:0 into on-spec methyl palmitate? Every number on this page comes from the unit's own model (noise off): the live simulator, or full campaigns run in node (tabs/effic/tools/efcomp.js). Values marked assumed are not from the model or the report.

    1 Definition and priorities · 2 Chains multiply · 3 Live KPIs · 4 Energy balance · 5 Model sweeps · 6 Rules of thumb vs model · 7 Options and money · 8 Constraint pushing · 9 Run your own campaign · 10 Limits and assumed values

    1 · What efficiency means for a batch column

    Efficiency is useful output per unit of what we spend. A continuous unit lines out and is judged per hour. A batch column never lines out: the pot gets heavier, the temperatures climb and the product purity falls during the cut. So we judge one whole campaign (total reflux → off-cut → product cut → stop) and divide by the product it made:

    • Energy per kg = ∫Q dt ÷ kg in TK-202 (kWh/kg). Q is the reboiler duty (JIC-101); the electricity into HE-101 is larger because the hot-oil loop loses heat.
    • Recovery of C16:0 = C16:0 in TK-202 ÷ C16:0 charged. What is not recovered sits in TK-201 (off-cut) and in the residue.
    • Productivity CAP = kg on-spec ÷ cutting hours (kg/h), and column-hours per campaign. Time is the scarce resource of a single pilot column.
    • Ester lost to the vacuum trap (uncondensed vapour through VP-101): a loss and a hazard at the same time.

    Efficiency is the sixth priority. We push it only inside the limits set by the first five:

    2 · Chains multiply

    The overall efficiency of a campaign is a product of links. A weak link cannot be made up by a strong one: 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.73.

    η = ηrecovery (C16:0 in on-spec product ÷ C16:0 charged) × ηtime (cutting hours ÷ whole cycle including turnaround) × ηenergy (heat that boils ester ÷ electricity into HE-101).

    assumed

    3 · Live KPIs of the running campaign

    From the live simulator (DCS console). Energy is integrated from the 5-s trend record since the campaign started (first distillate to TK-201). Run the campaign exercise and watch these numbers move. The right-hand column is the reference campaign A of the model.

    4 · Energy balance: hot oil, pot and condenser

    Where does the electricity go? The Sankey diagram follows the heat from HE-101 through the hot-oil loop and D-102 into the pot, up the column and out through E-103. Widths are to scale.

    Same relations as the model step: hot-oil loop loss 0.004 kW/K × (Toil − 30 °C), pot loss 0.0006 kW/K × (Tpot − 30 °C) assumed; "column internal" is the change of latent heat between the pot vapour (C16/C18-rich) and the overhead vapour (lighter), which the lumped model does not put anywhere else.

    5 · Model sweeps: one handle at a time

    Each row is one full campaign from the design state at total reflux (3 kW, 160 mbar, R 15 off-cut, R 10 product, switch when D-104 light esters < 4 %, stop when the cumulative TK-202 purity falls below 99.0 %). Only the named handle changes. kWh/kg counts the electricity into HE-101 per kg of on-spec product; "–" means the cut never reached 99.0 %.

    7 · Options sized in money

    Each option is taken from a model run above (no new physics). Electricity counts HE-101 plus the motors (assumed loads) during the cutting hours.

    assumed assumed

    8 · Constraint pushing: duty close to the flooding limit

    The fastest campaign uses the most duty the column can take. The limit is flooding: above ≈ 80 % of the flooding index the packing efficiency falls in the model, and above 100 % the column is flooded. The index is not steady: feed, foaming and duty noise move it. Choose a back-off of z standard deviations: the average sits at limit − z·σ.

    assumed

    9 · Run your own campaign

    One campaign on a copy of the model (≈ 10–20 s in the browser; the live simulator is not touched).

    10 · Limits of this page and assumed values

    • All campaigns start from the design state at total reflux; the start-up to total reflux (≈ in the model, SOP tab) and the turnaround are not in the cut-hours.
    • The electricity of VP-101, P-108, P-101 and P-104, the tariff, the campaigns per year, the turnaround, the σ of the flooding index and the 50 % insulation gain are assumed. Vapour pressures, ΔHv, packing F-max, condenser capacity (2.5× load) and the heat-loss coefficients are model assumptions (Process tab).
    • The model has no price for C16:0, off-cut or residue, so "profit" here is energy and time only. Raising R2 from 6 to 10 buys kg more product for kWh more electricity and h more column time ( kWh per extra kg): whether that pays depends on the product price, which the model does not know.
    • No campaign in the sweeps lost ester to the vacuum trap: the condenser has 2.5× capacity in the model. Losses there come from upsets (cooling water, vacuum), not from normal handles.

    SOP · standard operating procedures for C-101

    Fourteen written procedures for the vacuum batch column, from the walk-down to lockout. Limits are read from the page (alarm list, SIS-100 settings); the times and values come from scripted runs of the model (tabs/sop/tools/spcomp.js, noise off) and from reference campaign A. Values marked assumed are not from the model or the report.

    1 What an SOP is · 2 Format · 3 Register · 4 Viewer · 5 Writing rules · 6 Life cycle · 7 Model evidence

    1 · What an SOP is and which activities need one

    A standard operating procedure is the written, approved way to do one task on the unit, step by step, with the limits and the reasons. It is how the design intent (Design, Control and HAZOP tabs) reaches the operator at 3 a.m. OSHA PSM 29 CFR 1910.119(f) asks for written operating procedures that cover each operating phase, the operating limits, safety and health considerations and the safety systems, kept where operators can read them, reviewed as often as needed and certified annually. Lockout/tagout, opening process equipment and entry are covered by safe work practices.

    A batch unit spends most of its life in transitions (charge, evacuate, heat, cut, switch, cool, break vacuum, discharge), so it needs more procedures than a continuous unit of the same size.

    2 · Format of an SOP on this unit

    3 · Register

    Every SOP below opens in the viewer. Four carry a Practise (graded) button: it loads the matching graded procedure on the DCS console of this simulator.

    4 · Viewer

    5 · Writing rules: poor and better

    6 · Life cycle of a procedure

    A procedure is never finished: every change to the plant (MOC), every incident and every annual review sends it back to "Review". Operators who use it must be in the review — they know where it is wrong.

    7 · Model evidence behind the numbers

    Scripted runs follow the steps of the graded procedures of the simulator (start-up from cold, shutdown from the end of campaign A, loss of tempered water during the product cut). Real plant times will differ: the model has no operator delay, an assumed hot-oil inventory and assumed heat losses.

    Trainee workbook · Vacuum Batch Distillation Ver 1

    Work through Parts A to G in order. Record answers and evidence (screenshots, CSV files) as you go; your report is built from them.

    1 Purpose · 2 The unit · 3 Control scheme · 4 Safety systems · 5 Operating rules · 6 Activities A–G · 7 Grading · 8 Report checklist

    1 · Purpose

    This workbook trains you to operate, monitor and troubleshoot a pilot vacuum batch column that recovers methyl palmitate (C16:0, ≥ 99 %) from palm-oil biodiesel. By the end you should be able to:

    1. Read the P&ID and the DCS displays and state the normal value and alarm limits of every key tag.
    2. Explain how pressure, duty, reflux ratio and the still composition set the temperatures, the cut rates and the purity, and predict the direction every key variable moves after a disturbance.
    3. Start the still from cold to total reflux without flooding, and run a full campaign (off-cut, product cut) to specification.
    4. Recognise an abnormal situation, make it safe first, then find the root cause with a systematic six-stage method.
    5. Explain why the pilot as built (on/off heating, no drum level control) could not follow the simulated campaign, and support an improvement with data.

    2 · The unit

    110 L of biodiesel is charged to the still D-101 and heated by hot oil (HE-101, P-101, TV-101) through the reboiler D-102. Vapour rises through the packed column C-101 (20 theoretical stages) to the total condenser E-103 cooled by tempered water at 60 °C. Condensate collects in D-104; P-104 returns reflux (FIC-104) and sends distillate (FIC-105) through the D-105 sample point to the diverter XV-107: TK-201 (off-cut), TK-202 (product) or closed (total reflux). VP-101 holds the vacuum; PIC-102 bleeds N₂ through PV-102 to hold 160 mbar at the top.

    Values are the model's start-of-campaign state with noise off and the reference campaign results.

    3 · Control scheme

    TIC-107Hot-oil supply temperatureHE-101 power— (heater off on trip)290 °C.

    4 · Safety systems

    SIS-100 protects the heating. Heating can be armed only with the permissives green; a trip turns HE-101 off, closes XV-101, sets JIC-101 to 0 % and closes XV-107 (total reflux) so the product tank is not spoiled. The first cause is latched as first out; reset is allowed when the cause has cleared and heating must be armed again.

    Alarm limits

    5 · Operating rules

    1. Cooling and vacuum first, heat last; heat off first, vacuum last.
    2. Cut the duty to 3 kW before the pot boils. 8 kW heats the pot quickly but floods the column once vapour appears.
    3. Read temperatures together with pressure. A pressure change moves every temperature.
    4. Do not cut on TI-104 alone. The lights sit in D-104 for about two hours after TI-104 reaches the C16 plateau: switch to the product on a D-105 sample (C≤C14 below about 4 %).
    5. Watch TI-103 in the product cut. It sees the C18 front first; stop before the composite falls below 99 %.
    6. After every HS-107 move, check WI-201 and WI-202.
    7. Keep the tempered water above 45 °C; never break vacuum with air, and never above 150 °C.
    8. Check two instruments before you believe one: FIC-104 + FIC-105 against the condensate rate (duty ÷ λ ≈ 38 kg/h at 3 kW), LIC-104 against the sight glass, TIC-107 against TI-108.

    6 · Activities

    Part A · Familiarisation (about 20 min)

    1. Read the Process tab parts 1–4; trace the ester, hot-oil, water, N₂ and vacuum paths on the P&ID.
    2. Visit the four DCS displays; sketch the temperature profile at total reflux and explain the step in it.
    3. Complete the DCS reading sheet (graded out of 15).
    4. Download a profile snapshot CSV.

    Part B · What-if predictions (about 20 min)

    Predict ↑ / ↓ / — for all eight variables before pressing Check my predictions. Explain every wrong prediction with a pressure, heat or mass balance.

    Part C · Cold startup (graded, limit 4 h simulated)

      Part D · The campaign (graded on product, limit 20 h simulated)

        Record the cut times, the masses of TK-201 and TK-202, every lab result and your reasons for each cut decision. Compare your result with the reference campaign on the Process tab.

        Part E · Training exercises

        For each exercise: first alarm and time, the first variable you noticed, what you did, and the recovery time in Debrief.

        Part F · Think EQUIPPED troubleshooting

        StageWhat you must produce
        1 EngageIs it an emergency? Keep running, go to total reflux, or stop heating — and why.
        2 DefineProblem statement (what, where, when, how much), IS / IS NOT table, target state.
        3 ExploreFundamentals (pressure, heat, mass balances, VLE), consistency checks between instruments, recent changes, trends, lab data.
        4 PlanAt least three hypotheses, each with a diagnostic action ordered by safety, time and cost.
        5 Do itCarry out the actions, name the root cause, fix it. Predict before each move.
        6 Look backPrediction vs result; a change that stops it happening again.

        Part G · Trend matching, scrambles and report data

        Match four unlabelled trend sets to their events and justify each from the six pens; order the scrambles. For Part D and one Part F case download the run data CSV (all data sets, 60 s) and the event log; plot TI-104, TI-103, WI-201, WI-202 and the lab results against time.
